title: The Periodic Table and Its Trends

cards.b: The periodic table is chemistry's most useful chart. With one glance you can guess how an element behaves, what it bonds with and what it looks like. It even let scientists predict elements before they were found.

Dmitri Mendeleev, 1869, arranged the known elements by increasing atomic mass and noticed that properties repeat at regular intervals. He left gaps for unknown elements and predicted their properties.

He predicted eka-aluminium. In 1875 Lecoq de Boisbaudran found gallium, matching the prediction closely. That success made the table famous.

Henry Moseley, 1913, used X-rays to show that the real ordering principle is atomic number (protons), not mass. The modern periodic law: properties are a periodic function of atomic number. This fixed oddities like tellurium and iodine, where mass order disagreed with properties.

• Periods: 7 horizontal rows. Same number of shells.
  • Groups: 18 vertical columns. Same outer electrons, similar chemistry.
  • Blocks: s, p, d, f, named after the orbital being filled.

Famous groups: Group 1 alkali metals (Li, Na, K), Group 2 alkaline earths, Group 17 halogens, Group 18 noble gases. Metals sit left and centre, non-metals right, with metalloids (like silicon) on the staircase between.

Atomic radius decreases across a period (left to right): more protons pull the same shell tighter. It increases down a group: extra shells are added.

So caesium is huge, fluorine is tiny.

Ionisation energy is the energy needed to remove an electron. It rises across a period and falls down a group. That is why Group 1 metals lose electrons so easily.

Electronegativity (Linus Pauling's scale) is the pull on shared electrons. It rises towards the top right. Fluorine is the most electronegative element (4.0).

Reactivity follows: metals get more reactive going down a group (K is more reactive than Na); non-metals get more reactive going up (F more than I).

Element X is in Period 3, Group 17. Which element? Chlorine. It has 7 outer electrons, so it is a reactive non-metal that forms X- ions and bonds with Group 1 metals like sodium to make NaCl.

Compare size: Na (Period 3, Group 1) vs Cl (Period 3, Group 17). Across the period size shrinks, so Na is larger than Cl. Compare Li and K: same group, K is lower, so K is larger and loses its electron more easily.

• Hydrogen is not an alkali metal, though placed in Group 1.
  • Mendeleev did not know protons. Atomic number came later.
  • Larger atoms are not harder to ionise. The outer electron is farther away and easier to remove.
  • There are 118 known elements, the last (oganesson) completing Period 7.

Meghnad Saha derived the Saha ionisation equation in 1920, explaining how atoms of different elements ionise at different star temperatures. It is the basis for reading the chemistry of stars.

India's coastal sands in Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Odisha are rich in monazite, a mineral holding rare-earth elements and thorium, which links the periodic table directly to India's nuclear plans.

• Mendeleev (1869) arranged by mass; Moseley (1913) showed atomic number is the true order.
  • 18 groups, 7 periods; groups share outer-electron count.
  • Radius falls across, rises down; ionisation energy and electronegativity rise across.
